properties.description:
Analyze the needs for the Graph editor before selecting a layout or implementation. Child of Develop the Graph editor view; outside the MVP.

Context
The user wants to discover nodes carrying a particular component, including Task transition nodes that correctly do not appear as Inputs or Tasks on the Activity board. They also want insight into component types, relation types, their instances and connections.

The proposed direction is a 2D graph view plus a focus graph view with the filter tool. Graph editor is the requested name. The first version is read-only, as agreed in Answer 11; future CRUD remains a motivation for the name.

Topics to resolve progressively
- Which nodes and relations belong to the initial graph when switching from Activity board; how the current view and buildspace affect that scope.
- How to discover component/relation types and their instances, including nodes not shown in Activity board.
- What identity and information each graph node and relation displays.
- Layout behavior and how focus, filtering and navigation affect it.
- Read-only inspection capabilities, responsiveness and observable acceptance criteria. First-version editing scope is settled in Answer 11.

Interview procedure
Ask one question at a time in chat. Append each question and the user's answer verbatim here, preserving wording and order. Keep interpretations and agreed outcomes separate from the transcript. Do not invent an answer or treat unanswered proposals as decisions. Image-generation rounds follow this task and use its agreed outcomes.

Interview transcript

Question 1 (verbatim)
When you open Graph editor from the Activity board, what should its initial scope be: the current view’s nodes, all nodes associated with The Broccoli buildspace, or a selected node and its surroundings?

Answer 1 (verbatim)
thats what i don't know yet but i feel like showing the node for the current view is kind of a hidden / confusing behavior.

Imagine as a user you are in activity board, you select graph you see activity board nodes. Ok. Then you go in repositories and you switch back to graph and you see this time repositories nodes. Same action, different results and also not really practical because i have to go to the view i want to the nodes of before going to the graph view.

It also assume the use cases is i want to see the nodes of one of the view in isolation when i probably want to see the nodes of the build space and probably even more to be honest. I probably want to see all the nodes and filter them.

The trade off however of "i want to see all the nodes" is that i presume we are instancing nodes in both relational engine front end side and service side lazily as we should for performance reason. So saying i want to see all the nodes is kind of a non answer aswell.

Analysis notes after Answer 1 — separate from the verbatim transcript
- The user rejects a graph scope silently inherited from whichever view was previously open. Access should not require visiting a different view first.
- The desired reach extends beyond one view's nodes, potentially beyond the current buildspace. Its exact boundary remains unresolved.
- The user raises lazy instantiation on both browser and service as a performance consideration. This is a hypothesis about the current implementation, not a verified fact.
- Assistant proposal for discussion: distinguish the nodes eligible to be discovered, those matching the filter, and those currently loaded/drawn. Broad discoverability need not mean constructing and displaying every node at once. Filtering must make coverage or incomplete discovery explicit. This proposal has not yet been accepted.

Question 2 (verbatim)
Should a filter such as “has Task transition” find every matching node in the chosen scope, including nodes that neither the browser nor the service has loaded yet?

Answer 2 (verbatim)
> Should a filter such as “has Task transition” find every matching node in the chosen scope, including nodes that neither the browser nor the service has loaded yet?



The sentence part



> such as “has Task transition”



Is really important there, the behavior is unrelated to a specific component type,  we definitly should not leak task transition into relational engine (relational engine behind the one responsible for the filter system in the first place).



Now the question is really good because its an ambiguity we did not address yet. Should filter be a tool that hide only the already "materialized" nodes that does not match the filter or should it have the responsability to fetch all the nodes that match it filter even the unmaterialized ones.



Lets take for example activity board (but its true for repositories and other views aswell), it technicly display a filtered set of potential node related to the buildspace the broccoli. We could imagine aswell for scaling purpose that we don't fetch all the task and input each time we open the activity board view.



Does it mean that behind the sscene our initial request when we open the activity board view is more restrictive and as we navigate for example to the older completed task the filter become less restrictive and that what trigger additional materialization ?



Does it mean that each the broccoli contributor implementation need to handle that part aswell with the inherent complexity that come with it ?

Analysis notes after Answer 2 — separate from the verbatim transcript
User constraint
Task transition was only an example. Relational Engine filtering must remain generic and must not contain component-specific domain knowledge. The semantics of filtering materialized nodes versus discovering unmaterialized matches remain unresolved.

Code observations (read-only inspection; no implementation changes)
- Systems/Depth3/HarnessApp/Depth1/Browser/activity-board.ts: the board sends the same query expression with revision/grouping information and a page limit of 50; responses include a next cursor.
- Systems/Depth3/HarnessApp/planning-activity.ts: the service builds eligible/projected collections from state.nodes, evaluates the query and then pages each collection. This browser paging does not establish lazy source-side materialization.
- Systems/Depth0/RelationEngine/relational-contributor.ts and relational-engine.ts: the generic resolve(query, service) hook allows queries to ask contributors for element selections beyond the currently available engine selection.
- Systems/Depth0/RelationEngine/Depth4/Querying/relational-query.ts: the generic element query contract has scope and predicates but no page limit or cursor. Existing collection paging and contributor resolution do not yet establish one complete end-to-end paged source query contract.

Assistant proposal for discussion, not yet accepted
A filter describes which results qualify. Query execution retrieves those results from sources. Navigation requests additional pages or regions of the same result set; it need not weaken the filter. For example, a closed-items query can retain the same scope and ordering while successive pages retrieve older matches. A backend may express its cursor as an additional storage condition without changing the user-visible filter.

The engine should own generic query semantics and coordinate execution, continuation, caching and invalidation through a shared contract. Contributors should expose their owned data through source capabilities; they should not each implement filter syntax, scroll behavior or view-specific loading policy. Common source access can be reused. Efficiently searching data not yet materialized requires source-side enumeration, indexes or query support; the engine cannot infer undiscoverable nodes. The exact source contract, completeness reporting and costs remain design questions.

Question 3 (verbatim)
Should we adopt that as a shared rule across views: filtering defines the result set, while navigation controls how much of it is loaded?

Answer 3 (verbatim)
> Some source-specific work is unavoidable: the engine cannot discover unmaterialized nodes unless their source can enumerate or search them. But contributors should not each reinvent filter parsing, pagination and scrolling behavior. Contributors using the same storage mechanism should share that access implementation. Efficient queries may also require indexes; pagination alone does not eliminate the cost of finding matches.



indeed i agree but i am a bit worried of the complexity contributor side if we defer to much on them. With the relational engine API / how contributor connect with the relational engine we should as much as possible provide the structure for them to be able to have to do minimal complexity on their side.



> Should we adopt that as a shared rule across views: filtering defines the result set, while navigation controls how much of it is loaded?



I wonder if we are not jumping of converting a pattern that seems to repeat itself for the uses cases we had until now into a rule. I would also say that ui is a layer above relational engine and basing how relational engine work on what we need from the ui seems like a dependency leak upward / a dependency inversion.

Analysis notes after Answer 3 — separate from the verbatim transcript
User constraints and challenge
- The engine API and contributor integration should supply as much shared structure as possible, minimizing contributor-side complexity rather than delegating the problem wholesale.
- The user challenges turning the pattern observed in current views into a general rule.
- The UI is above Relational Engine. Engine responsibilities must not depend on UI-specific navigation or presentation policies.
- Question 3's proposed shared rule is not accepted. Earlier proposed responsibility assignments remain provisional and must not be treated as architecture decisions.

Assistant correction and next investigation
A UI scenario can reveal a need without transferring UI policy into the engine. The architectural test is whether the proposed engine capability can be defined and justified for consumers without a UI. Scrolling behavior belongs to the UI; bounded or incremental access to query results could be an engine capability, but pagination is only one possible mechanism and no mechanism has been selected.

A general contributor query hook alone does not minimize contributor work. Identify the knowledge only a source owner can supply, and provide shared engine structure for the rest. The precise source operations and division of execution responsibilities remain open.

Before selecting a discovery/materialization contract, clarify whether the queryable domain includes nodes computed on demand without their own stored records. This affects what can be enumerated, searched or counted and what a contributor must describe. Question 4 explores that need independently of any view.

Question 4 (verbatim)
Should the engine also support discovering nodes that are computed on demand and have no stored record of their own?

Answer 4 (verbatim)
> For example, “scrolling requests another page” belongs to the UI. “A consumer can access query results without materializing the entire dataset” could be an engine requirement. Pagination would then be one possible implementation—not something we should establish from the scrolling example alone.



yep exactly



> Your contributor-complexity concern also changes the design approach. Providing a broad “resolve this query” hook can merely move the difficult work into every contributor. We should identify the knowledge only the contributor possesses, then have the engine supply the common structure and behavior around it. The exact division remains to be established.



Exactly aswell. i am sure there will be limitation and we might have tradeoff decision to make to balance out the thing but this part need to be really well though out.



> Should the engine also support discovering nodes that are computed on demand and have no stored record of their own?



yep i would say it seems pretty important to me.

Analysis notes after Answer 4 — separate from the verbatim transcript
Agreed principles
- Describe engine needs independently of UI behavior. Access to query results without materializing the entire dataset is an engine-level capability to pursue; scrolling behavior is UI policy. Pagination remains an unselected implementation option.
- Identify knowledge only the contributor possesses, and provide common engine structure and behavior around it to minimize contributor-side complexity. The precise division, limitations and tradeoffs need careful analysis.
- Discovery must support nodes computed on demand without a stored record of their own.

Still unresolved
The queryable universe, discovery guarantees, loading mechanism, source operations and exact contributor responsibilities are not settled. The earlier proposed universal navigation/filter rule remains unaccepted.

Next investigation
Use a concrete computed-node scenario to identify the source-specific knowledge, expected discovery behavior and costs. This is evidence for comparing possible contracts, not a decision to specialize the engine for that scenario.

Question 5 (verbatim)
What is one concrete example of a computed node, with no stored record of its own, that you would want the engine to discover?

Answer 5 (verbatim)
> What is one concrete example of a computed node, with no stored record of its own, that you would want the engine to discover?



Well i don't know which one is part of that "category" so i would have a hard time answering that. I would say however that the distinction is probably a bit tenuous by saying a "computed node" technicly every node is computed.



I also don't understand why you would ask that to be honest maybe go straight to the point for this one ?

Analysis notes after Answer 5 — separate from the verbatim transcript
User correction
The user cannot readily classify existing nodes as stored versus computed, questions the usefulness of that distinction because every node involves computation, and asks for the underlying point directly.

Assistant correction
Stored versus computed is not a proposed semantic classification of nodes. Asking the user to classify implementation examples was an indirect way of investigating discoverability and contributor obligations.

The actual open issue is whether every contributor must be able to enumerate its complete domain, possibly progressively, or whether some contributors may need specific constraints before discovery is possible. That affects the completeness an unconstrained query can promise and the minimum contract contributors must implement. Enumeration here does not require constructing or loading every node simultaneously. Neither alternative is selected.

Question 6 asks that contract question directly. No implementation changes or additional node categories are authorized by this discussion.

Question 6 (verbatim)
Must every contributor support listing all the nodes it can expose, or can a contributor require a more specific query before it can discover nodes?

Answer 6 (verbatim)
i would say contributor probably need to provide the component type / data type and everything type related so the filter can discover what it can filter / request at the very least. I would not shutdown lazy load completly for this group of nodes but if a contributor contribute nothing by default it could prove difficult.

Doesn't mean that the implemenation need to go contributor -> relational engine though, relational engine could request those group of nodes through the same mechanism it use to fetch other nodes.

I would not exclude other mechanism though but i can't provide more context currently with my understanding.

Analysis notes after Answer 6 — separate from the verbatim transcript
User direction
- At minimum, contributor type information (component types, data types and other type-related information) should be discoverable so filtering can learn what it can filter or request.
- Type-related nodes may themselves be loaded lazily. A contributor exposing nothing by default may make discovery difficult, but eager loading of every type is not required by this answer.
- Do not assume contributors must push declarations into the engine. The engine could request those nodes through the same mechanism used for other nodes.
- Other mechanisms remain possible; the user cannot provide further context on this contract at present.

Unresolved design work
The direction is discoverability of available query vocabulary, not a selected bootstrap protocol, dedicated metadata API or separate type-loading channel. A generic entry path must be investigated without imposing component-specific knowledge on the engine.
This answer does not establish that every instance can be enumerated. Instance completeness, discovery limits and contributor obligations remain open for technical investigation alongside the accepted goal of minimizing contributor complexity.

Next interview topic
Move back to an observable graph exploration need: connections crossing the current filter boundary. This does not settle engine loading policy or the initial graph scope. Question 7 asks about the graph's presentation and exploration behavior.

Question 7 (verbatim)
If a node matches your filter but a connected node does not, should the graph show that connection immediately, or only when you explicitly explore that node’s relations?

Answer 7 (verbatim)
i would say filter is there to restrict  what is shown including edge type.

so if there is a node that does not match the filter but an edge that does then we show the edge and we show maybe a placeholder node that say filtered instead of the node ?

Analysis notes after Answer 7 — separate from the verbatim transcript
User direction
- Filtering restricts what is shown, including edge types.
- A matching edge should remain visible even when a connected node does not match the filter.
- The user proposes, tentatively, a placeholder labeled Filtered in place of the excluded node. The placeholder presentation needs refinement.

Assistant interpretation for discussion
Node visibility and edge visibility should be evaluated separately; an edge is not automatically omitted merely because one endpoint fails the node filter.
A proposed placeholder would represent the real edge endpoint in the graph presentation, without showing the excluded node's content. It would not create a synthetic node in the underlying relational model.
The placeholder's identity and grouping need clarification: multiple matching edges may share the same excluded endpoint. Question 8 asks whether that shared endpoint remains visible as one shared placeholder.

No final placeholder interaction, styling or loading protocol is selected.

Question 8 (verbatim)
Should multiple visible edges to the same filtered-out node meet at one shared “Filtered” placeholder?

Answer 8 (verbatim)
yes.

Analysis notes after Answer 8 — separate from the verbatim transcript
Agreed
- Multiple visible edges to the same filtered-out node meet at one shared “Filtered” placeholder.

Assistant interpretation
This preserves the shared endpoint of those edges. Distinct excluded nodes remain distinct placeholders rather than being merged into one endpoint.

Placeholder styling, interaction and loading behavior remain unresolved. The next question returns to the information displayed for ordinary nodes.

Question 9 (verbatim)
For an unfiltered node, what information should be visible without selecting it?

Answer 9 (verbatim)
this one is tricky, a label with a text is pretty much out of the question i would say because i can't find a solution personnaly to decide where the label should come from that scale.



showing the full information on the node by default would not scale well for massive ammount of nodes. This one is a really interesting question we need to find an anwer to though and quite the challenging ui subject.



The constraint i would work around are :

- it need to scale for very large amount of varied nodes
- text for me doesn't not scale with large amount of node, which leave color, shape, animation, size, (any other visual aspect we can work with ?)
- it shouldn't require of the user to have to define how thing are represented by default but still be usable.
- it need to be / stay readable as we dezoom.



I don't have a specific system in mind yet though that match those constraint.



Any idea ?

Analysis notes after Answer 9 — separate from the verbatim transcript
User constraints and position
- The presentation must scale to very large numbers of varied nodes.
- The user sees no scalable general rule for sourcing a node label and does not want full node information displayed by default.
- Explore visual channels beyond text, including color, shape, animation and size.
- The default presentation must be usable without requiring the user to configure representations.
- The graph must remain readable when zooming out.
- No representation system has been selected. The user asks for ideas.

Assistant proposal for discussion — not accepted design
Explore a representation that changes with zoom. Separate fitting a large graph on screen from explaining varied node content.
At an overview level, consider explicit aggregates showing regions, density and connections. At a closer level, show individual simple marks and actual edges. Inspection exposes the real component/property structure and canonical identity without inventing a universal title.
A default could emphasize connectivity; optional visual comparisons could use contributed component metadata. A node may have multiple components, so this does not establish one primary type or a distinct color/shape per component combination.
Other candidate channels include position, proximity, enclosure, texture, outline and edge style. Keep encodings limited and explainable; reserve motion for brief transitions or interaction feedback.
Aggregation would be a presentation operation, not a change to filtering or the underlying graph. It must be distinguishable from the agreed Filtered endpoint placeholder and support access to every represented node and exact relation. Partial query coverage must remain explicit.
Grouping criteria, layout, encodings and loading mechanisms remain unresolved. Research precedent: multiscale aggregation in ZAME (https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/publication/zame-interactive-large-scale-graph-visualization/); its matrix representation is not selected for this project.
Question 10 asks only whether aggregation is acceptable when zooming out. A positive answer would not approve the entire proposal or any particular grouping algorithm.

Question 10 (verbatim)
When zooming out, would you accept a group of nodes becoming one visibly aggregated mark, provided zooming in restores the individual nodes and their exact connections?

Answer 10 (verbatim)
> epresentation that changes with zoom



I am on the fence for this one, i think we need to experiment during the image gen rounds task to decide how we solve the subject and iterating in the question would be a waste of time.

Analysis notes after Answer 10 — separate from the verbatim transcript
User direction
- Defer how to represent large numbers of varied nodes, including changes of representation with zoom, to concrete experiments in the image-generation rounds.
- Further interview questions on that visual solution are not useful at this stage.
- Zoom-dependent representation and aggregation are not accepted decisions.

Follow-through
The successor image-generation task now explicitly owns exploration of these visual alternatives under the constraints in Answer 9. Keep this subject open until the user has reviewed concrete examples.
Question 11 moves to the first version's functional scope; it does not ask for another visual-design decision.

Question 11 (verbatim)
For the first version, do you want to create and edit nodes and relations from the graph, or keep it focused on exploration and inspection?

Answer 11 (verbatim)
read only for the first version.

Analysis notes after Answer 11 — separate from the verbatim transcript
Agreed
- The first Graph editor version is read-only: exploration and inspection of nodes and relations.
- Creating, editing and deleting graph data are outside the first version's scope. The name Graph editor remains appropriate to the intended future direction.

Follow-through
The development and image-generation tasks now refer to this agreed first-version scope. Visual representation remains deferred to image-generation experiments as directed in Answer 10.
Question 12 concerns focus navigation. It does not change the agreed filter and filtered-endpoint behavior or prescribe an engine loading mechanism.

Question 12 (verbatim)
For the focus view, should it start with the selected node and its direct connections, then let you expand outward as needed?

Answer 12 (verbatim)
Question again is interesting again and my answer answer a bit of the same question for the graph editor view.

I think that we open the unfiltered view for the first time the filter should by default include an operator materialized(true) so it shows only what we already know by default and keep the view content correct with the filter.

Focus tab would be the same thing with materialized(true) && node.url("<an expression that is either the selected node url or that refer to the source selection of what focused") .

That way we use the same logic for both and we have something that doesn't fetch by default more than what we start with.

Analysis notes after Answer 12 — separate from the verbatim transcript
User direction
- On first opening the otherwise unfiltered graph view, initialize the visible filter with materialized(true), restricting the view to what is already known.
- Focus uses the same mechanism, adding node.url(...) with an expression for the selected node URL or a reference to the source selection.
- Both views use shared filter logic and do not fetch additional unknown graph content by default.
- The materialized restriction is explicit in the filter, so the displayed result remains consistent with it.
- This answers part of the initial-scope question. It does not approve the earlier proposed one-hop expansion behavior.

Implementation observations — not design constraints
The inspected current query contracts (Systems/Depth0/RelationEngine/Depth4/Querying/relational-query.ts and query-language.ts) do not define the proposed materialized(true) or node.url(...) operators. The desired semantics are being recorded for later design, not claimed as implemented behavior.

Open semantics
- Define which materialization boundary is meant: browser-local knowledge or service knowledge also available to the browser.
- Evaluating a materialized-only query must not first trigger discovery/materialization and then filter the enlarged result. The restriction must govern query execution as well as the visible result.
- An exact node URL condition identifies a node; it does not by itself establish which connections or neighboring nodes the focus view includes. Preserve that question as open alongside the already agreed node/edge filtering and endpoint placeholder behavior.
- The source-selection reference mechanism, temporal behavior of materialized membership, and the effect of changing/removing this restriction remain to be designed.
- UI-selected defaults must not introduce view vocabulary or policies into the generic engine contract.

Question 13 (verbatim)
Should materialized(true) mean already present in the browser, or include nodes already materialized by the service that the browser has not received yet?

Answer 13 (verbatim)
> **Focus:** the same restriction, combined with the selected node URL or source-selection reference.  



selected node(s).



> Should `materialized(true)` mean already present in the browser, or include nodes already materialized by the service that the browser has not received yet?  



you cooking my boy, yeah it was a bit of an oversimplification, indeed materialized should probably not take a bool but probably the relational engine instance. I would probably start with the front end one as the default filter.

Analysis notes after Answer 13 — separate from the verbatim transcript
User direction and corrections
- Focus supports selected node(s), not only one selected node. The selection may contain multiple nodes.
- Materialization should be relative to a specified Relational Engine instance. The proposed operator argument is that instance, replacing the earlier Boolean shorthand.
- Start with the frontend engine instance as the default filter boundary.

Current interpretation
The generic materialization predicate identifies which engine instance's known elements are eligible. The Graph editor and focus UI supply the frontend instance as their initial default. The engine contract must not hard-code frontend or view-specific policy.
Focus adds either selected node identities or an expression referring to the source selection, preserving support for more than one node.
The earlier materialized(true) expressions remain only in the historical transcript and notes. Current direction is an instance-relative predicate; exact syntax and how an engine instance is referenced remain implementation design questions.
This resolves the default browser/service boundary in Question 13. It does not yet decide how the focus filter selects edges or includes neighbors; Question 14 addresses that relationship explicitly.
No source code or query operator has been implemented in this interview.

Question 14 (verbatim)
Within that materialized set, should focus include edges touching any selected node, showing a shared “Filtered” placeholder wherever the other endpoint is excluded?

Answer 14 (verbatim)
probably would start with all the materialized edge type + materialized nodes directly connected to the focused node(s).

Filter content however should not be a combination of the url. I probably would want an operator in the idea of :
"maxDistnace(1)"

I would however not use the term distance but a term in the lexical field of graph with no connotation to any domain outside of that ideally.

Analysis notes after Answer 14 — separate from the verbatim transcript
User direction
- Start focus with all materialized edge types and materialized nodes directly connected to the focused node(s).
- Express that neighborhood through a traversal-limit operator, not an enumerated combination of node URLs.
- The user's illustrative spelling maxDistnace(1) conveys a one-edge limit. They want a graph-oriented term instead of distance.

Assistant interpretation and proposal — not yet accepted naming
- Treat the focused nodes as a set of traversal roots. The generic query receives that set or an expression resolving it; the UI supplies the selection without introducing focus-tab vocabulary into the engine.
- Interpret all materialized edge types as eligible relation types for this traversal, not a request to add unrelated edge instances or all edge-type definition nodes to the focus result.
- Propose maxTraversalDepth(1). Define a node's depth as the minimum number of traversed edges from any root: depth 0 includes the roots, depth 1 includes their direct neighbors, and depth 2 adds nodes reachable through one intermediate node. The limit includes all depths up to the specified value.
- This is a proposed name and semantic formulation, not a selected implementation or traversal algorithm. Graph APIs use comparable depth limits; terminology reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/neptune-analytics/latest/userguide/bfs-standard.html.
- Retain the engine-instance materialization restriction, initially the frontend instance. Traversal must not discover/materialize additional nodes merely to evaluate this default query.
- Directly connected eligible materialized nodes are ordinary visible nodes. The existing shared Filtered placeholder rule still applies when another node filter excludes an endpoint of a visible edge.
- Direction of traversal remains open. Question 15 asks about the default for directed relations.
- Boundary-edge inclusion and how node/edge predicates affect traversal remain technical semantics to resolve; do not silently assume that every edge incident to every included neighbor belongs in the result.

Question 15 (verbatim)
Should traversal follow both incoming and outgoing edges by default?

Answer 15 (verbatim)
> `maxTraversalDepth`  



yep i like that.



yep i think we would probably have an additional operator if we want to restrict direction.

Analysis notes after Answer 15 — separate from the verbatim transcript
Agreed
- maxTraversalDepth is the accepted operator name.
- Traversal follows incoming and outgoing edges by default.
- Restricting traversal direction should use an additional operator.

Implementation/design boundaries
The name and default direction are settled. The direction operator's name and exact contract remain open. Bidirectional traversal does not change the underlying direction or identity of an edge.
The next semantic question is whether a node predicate only removes a node from the displayed result or also blocks traversal through it. This must be explicit before combining node filters with traversal-depth constraints. Question 16 uses a fully materialized three-node example, with both edges allowed, to isolate that behavior from loading and edge filtering.
No implementation has started; visual representation remains for the image-generation rounds.

Question 16 (verbatim)
With A focused in materialized A—B—C and both edges allowed, should maxTraversalDepth(2) show matching C even when B is excluded by the node filter?

Answer 16 (verbatim)
can you frame the question with the actual query example instead of only a sentence because my answer depend on the actual filter.

Analysis notes after Answer 16 — separate from the verbatim transcript
- The user requests a concrete query example because their answer depends on the actual filter expression.
- This is a request to clarify Question 16, not an answer establishing traversal/filter semantics.
- Question 17 reframes that same issue with explicit starting nodes, node and edge predicates, and the placement of the B exclusion as a sibling conjunction.
- The example uses the proposed operators. It does not claim implemented syntax or establish a finalized query wrapper/API.

Question 17 (verbatim)
Using the operators we are designing, assume the graph is `A—B—C`. A, B and C stand for node URLs; all three nodes and both edges are materialized in the frontend engine.

The concrete query example is:

```text
startNodes: {A}

nodeFilter:
  materialized(frontendEngine)
  && maxTraversalDepth(2)
  && !node.url(B)

edgeFilter:
  materialized(frontendEngine)
```

Here, excluding B is a separate `&&` condition, not a predicate nested inside `maxTraversalDepth`. The notation for supplying starting nodes and separating node/edge filters is illustrative, not a finalized API.

Does C pass this node filter and appear normally, while B appears as a “Filtered” placeholder?

Answer 17 (verbatim)
okay how you structure the query worry me a bit. You make three group (start node) / node filter / edge filter.

i don't want three filter, i want an unified filter query system so considering what you want to express it should be expressed as a one liner with property && || operator.

Analysis notes after Answer 17 — separate from the verbatim transcript
User correction
- Require one unified filter-query system.
- Express the query as a single expression composed from properties and Boolean operators such as && and ||.
- Reject the assistant's prior division into startNodes, nodeFilter and edgeFilter groups.

Follow-through
The earlier three-section example is withdrawn as a proposed contract; it remains only as verbatim interview history. The parent and image-generation tasks now explicitly require one unified expression.
The behavior of traversal through excluded nodes is still unanswered. Question 18 restates that behavior using a unified expression.
The new isNode()/isEdge() predicates and from: argument are illustrative proposed syntax, not accepted requirements. A starting-node set or source-selection reference must be expressible within the unified query rather than imposed as a separate filter category.
The root-selection predicate inside traversal and the candidate-node exclusion outside it are different expression positions. Do not silently infer execution order from the written order of && terms or claim a query result before its semantics are agreed.
No implementation has started.

Question 18 (verbatim)
For the same fully materialized A—B—C example, here is a single proposed expression:

```text
materialized(frontendEngine) && (isEdge() || (isNode() && maxTraversalDepth(2, from: node.url(A)) && !node.url(B)))
```

The starting-node condition is an argument of the traversal operator, inside the expression. isNode(), isEdge() and the from: argument are illustrative spellings, not agreed API names. This expression includes materialized edges, plus materialized nodes satisfying the depth limit and B exclusion.

With this expression, should C match through B, while B itself is shown as a “Filtered” placeholder?

Answer 18 (verbatim)
yep if i understood correctly the expressing we start from the focused node a and look two edge away any node or edge except b so it match the expected behavior of seeing everything and having the filtered placeholder node for b because we excluded it but we don't want edge without a node representation on both end placeholder or not.

Unrelated bu i think we need to improve the ui component for filter because it would be annoying for the user to start with a non empty field but as annoying to not have access and control to the intial filter. I want to include that as part of the need analysis, image gen, dev scope.

Analysis notes after Answer 18 — separate from the verbatim transcript
Accepted intended behavior
- For the A—B—C example rooted at A with a depth limit of 2, excluding B from the result does not prevent matching C through B.
- B has a Filtered placeholder when visible edges refer to it. Every displayed edge must have a node representation at both endpoints, either the visible node or its shared placeholder.
- The user's intended depth restriction applies to nodes and edges.

Correction to the assistant's previous example
The previous isEdge() disjunct accepted every materialized edge, even outside the traversal limit. That expression did not fully match the behavior the user understood and approved. Preserve the user's stated intent, not the defective example, as the requirement.
A corrected illustrative shape puts maxTraversalDepth outside that disjunction: materialized(frontendEngine) && maxTraversalDepth(2, from: node.url(A)) && !(isNode() && node.url(B)).
This is still proposed syntax. The exact treatment of boundary edges remains to be defined; do not claim the earlier expression already enforced it.

New scope: improve the existing filter UI component
- Include this work in need analysis, image-generation rounds and development.
- Address the tension between an annoying prefilled initial field and the user's need to access and control the initial filter.
- Explore a comfortable initial entry experience while making the active initial restrictions discoverable, inspectable and modifiable.
- Preserve the unified query requirement. A presentation that makes editing easier must not introduce hidden independent filters or inaccessible constraints.
- Extend/rework the shared filter UI component; no separate graph-only filter implementation or new component is approved by this request.
- The UI arrangement is unresolved and should be explored with concrete visual alternatives in the image-generation task. Query editing does not change the read-only scope for graph data.

Next semantic question
The node-exclusion case is settled. Question 19 isolates excluding an edge from the same fully materialized graph, with no node excluded. The edge predicate and from: syntax remain illustrative. This asks whether an ordinary edge predicate changes traversal reachability or only result membership.

Question 19 (verbatim)
For the next case, use the same fully materialized A—B—C graph, with AB standing for the URL of the A—B edge. Using the proposed syntax:

```text
materialized(frontendEngine) && maxTraversalDepth(2, from: node.url(A)) && !(isEdge() && edge.url(AB))
```

Should excluding AB only hide that edge, leaving B and C reachable, or should it also block traversal through AB?

Answer 19 (verbatim)
> My previous `isEdge()` branch accidentally bypassed the depth limit; I’ve corrected that in the notes.  



Good catch.



> Should excluding AB only hide that edge, leaving B and C reachable, or should it also block traversal through AB?



I feel like you are trying to resolve an ambiguity through multiple example based on the two previous question maybe we could address it directly ?



unrelated but lets say the user remove materialized it should not mean we look for everynode recursively through the relational engine graph azll the nodes that match the other operators.



Which mean that filter might not be the right term to describe our ui component in the end. Because the expression is not exclusively substractive. Materialized would be additive.

Analysis notes after Answer 19 — separate from the verbatim transcript
User direction
- Address the underlying query-semantics ambiguity directly instead of deriving it through repeated node/edge examples.
- Removing materialized must not implicitly trigger a recursive search of all graph nodes matching the remaining operators.
- The expression is not exclusively subtractive. The user identifies materialized as additive.
- Reconsider Filter as the name of the shared UI component, because it must cover more than restricting an existing set.

Correction to the earlier assistant framing
Do not model materialized solely as a Boolean predicate restricting an implicitly universal candidate graph. It explicitly contributes/selects known elements relative to an engine instance. Removing that contribution does not authorize discovery over an implicit universal graph.
The node-exclusion behavior accepted in Answer 18 is grounded in that example and expression scope; it must not be generalized to every condition regardless of where it is applied.
Question 19 received a request to establish the general model, not an answer selecting a new edge-exclusion rule.

Assistant proposal for discussion — not accepted semantics
The ambiguity is which graph a traversal may explore versus which elements the whole query returns.
Within one unified expression, source-selection operators can supply elements, traversal can explore from explicit inputs under bounds, and predicates can restrict chosen inputs or results.
Candidate scoping rule: traversal takes an explicit input expression; conditions applied to that input control available paths, while conditions applied to the traversal result control returned elements. This can express both behaviors without implicit ordering-dependent side effects in &&/||.
These are roles within one expression, not separate start/node/edge filter groups or separate UI fields.
If removing source-producing terms leaves no source, the empty/invalid-query behavior remains to be defined; it must never default to an implicit recursive scan.
Query editor is a proposed component name, not yet selected. The exact syntax and interaction of source-producing operators, traversal and Boolean composition remain to be designed.

Follow-through
The development and image-generation descriptions now include additive/source-selection semantics, the prohibition on implicit recursive discovery when materialized is removed, and exploration of a more accurate shared-component name.
Question 20 directly asks about expression scope. It replaces further piecemeal node/edge examples.

Question 20 (verbatim)
Should traversal take an explicit input expression, with conditions on that input controlling exploration and conditions on its result controlling what is returned?

Answer 20 (verbatim)
> These are roles within **one expression**. Removing `materialized` removes that contribution; it must not introduce an implicit “search the entire graph” source. What happens when no source remains still needs defining.  



Yep you outline a really important aspect in our design, explicity. This avoid the user triggering think it does not expect would be nefarious. (a full recursive request across all connected relational engine instance would be catastrophic at large scale).



Doesn't mean we don't need to design additional system in the futur to prevent unwanted effect but that would be our first layer of defense.



> Query editor



yep agree with the query editor.



> These are roles within **one expression**  



yep it would also help to make those broad role category explicit for the user aswell, i am thinking green for additive, red for restrictive, (yellow for mutating ?) as my first thought but we probably want to iterate on that (the group and how we present them to the user).



> My proposed resolution is to make the scope of each condition explicit: excluding something from a traversal’s input affects available paths; excluding it from the traversal’s result affects what is returned. This avoids deriving behavior from the written order of `&&` conditions.  



> Should traversal take an explicit input expression, with conditions on that input controlling exploration and conditions on its result controlling what is returned?



I think you are onto something there but i need you to expand a bit so i can confirm my intuition.

Analysis notes after Answer 20 — separate from the verbatim transcript
Accepted direction
- Explicitness is a design requirement and a first layer of protection against unintended effects, particularly recursive requests across connected engine instances at scale.
- Removing materialized must not create an implicit universal recursive search.
- Query editor is the accepted name for the shared UI component.
- Make broad operator roles understandable to the user within the unified expression.

Proposals to explore in image-generation rounds
- The user's initial visual idea is green for additive, red for restrictive and possibly yellow for mutating roles.
- Both the role categories and their visual representation remain exploratory; these colors are not an accepted final mapping.
- The meaning and inclusion of a mutating role remain unresolved. The first Graph editor version remains read-only; this suggestion does not authorize graph mutations.
- Additional future protections may be needed beyond explicitness, but no particular mechanism is selected here.

Requested clarification
The user has not yet accepted the input/result scoping model and asks for an expanded explanation before confirming. Keep that model proposed.

Expanded assistant proposal — not implemented or accepted architecture
Each operation receives an input defined by a nested expression. A condition's scope is given by the expression it belongs to, not the textual evaluation order of && terms.
For illustration only, give maxTraversalDepth explicit from: and within: operands. within: supplies the graph available to traversal; from: identifies roots within that graph. These operands are part of the one expression, not separate filter fields.
For this candidate model, a traversal step uses an admitted edge between admitted nodes. An excluded endpoint's identity in an edge record does not authorize traversal through it. A display placeholder does not become an engine node or a traversal path.

Illustration with fully materialized A—B—C and A as the root
Result exclusion:
maxTraversalDepth(2, from: node.url(A), within: materialized(frontendEngine)) && !(isNode() && node.url(B))
The traversal input includes B, so C is reachable. The outer condition removes B from returned nodes. The two visible edges use one shared Filtered placeholder for B.

Input exclusion:
maxTraversalDepth(2, from: node.url(A), within: materialized(frontendEngine) && !(isNode() && node.url(B)))
B is excluded from the graph admitted for traversal. The path from A through B to C is unavailable, so C is not reached through that path. This does not delete B or its edges from the underlying graph.

The expressions differ in nesting and therefore in the input supplied to the operation. Their meaning is not an imperative sequence based on the order of && terms. Generic operator/source contracts must express this without UI-specific vocabulary.
Both examples have an explicit materialized source. Removing that source cannot silently authorize access to other engine instances or recursive discovery. Missing-source behavior still needs definition.
The exact operator signature, typing of expression results and treatment of boundary edges remain design questions. These examples explain a candidate semantic model, not an implemented query language.

Question 21 (verbatim)
Does this match your intuition: nesting a condition in the traversal input constrains exploration, while applying it to the traversal result only controls what is returned?

Answer 21 (verbatim)
too in depth for a first explanation, i have a hard time understanding the core idea(s) the nuance compared to what we were up until now ?

Clarification status
The user requested a simpler first explanation. The proposed traversal-input/result distinction remains unconfirmed; no new semantics or syntax were accepted.

Simplified explanation presented with Question 22 (verbatim)
The core distinction is **hiding something versus preventing exploration through it**.

With **A — B — C**, starting from A:

- **What we already agreed:** hide B, but still reach C through it. B appears as a “Filtered” placeholder.
- **The additional proposal:** allow “don’t go through B.” Then C cannot be reached along that path.

The nesting idea was simply a proposed way to express those different intentions **within one query**. We haven’t agreed on the syntax.

Question 22 (verbatim)
Do you want the query to support both intentions?

Answer 22 (verbatim)
ok that was not the intuition i had but you are right its not because something is hidden in what we show at the end that it mean we don't have to query it to solve the full request and the nuance as you can see with me requiring two rounds of clarification can be quite difficult to expose to the user explicitly.

Is that what you were trying to tell me ?

Assistant clarification (verbatim)
Yes. **A node can be necessary to answer a query without appearing in its result.**

For **A — B — C**, the engine may need to examine B to reach C, even though you excluded B from the displayed result. That examination still stays within the query’s explicitly permitted scope.

My additional proposal was to also let you express “don’t explore through B,” which changes what can be reached.

And yes, communicating that difference is the difficult part. I jumped into syntax too early. We should preserve the distinction in our analysis and experiment with how to expose it clearly during the design rounds.

Analysis status after Answer 22
The user recognizes that a node excluded from the displayed result may still need to be queried to resolve the overall request, and highlights the difficulty of explaining that distinction. They asked for confirmation of that understanding. This does not yet accept a particular traversal-input syntax or explicitly confirm the additional capability to prohibit traversal through excluded elements. Preserve the existing explicit-source limits. Presenting the distinction clearly remains an open Query editor design concern; the assistant proposes exploring it during the design rounds. No new interview question was asked in this clarification response.

User follow-up after clarification of Answer 22 (verbatim)
ok we can move on then.

Analysis status
The user agreed to move on after the distinction between examining nodes and including them in results was clarified. Carry that distinction forward; the proposed nesting syntax remains unselected. Continue with the unresolved no-source behavior.

Context for Question 23 (verbatim)
Suppose you change this query (illustrative syntax):

```text
materialized(frontendEngine) && isNode()
```

into:

```text
isNode()
```

You’ve kept a restriction but removed the only source. We’ve agreed this must not trigger discovery across the whole graph.

Question 23 (verbatim)
Should the Query editor report “No source specified,” or treat this as a valid query returning nothing?

Assistant recommendation accompanying Question 23 (verbatim)
I favor reporting the missing source, so it’s distinguishable from a query that searched its source and found no matches.

Answer 23 (verbatim)
for the mvp i would keep it simple and make it a valid query honestly. i understand the idea you are coming from but i don't think the value is worth the hassle at this stage.

Agreed outcome after Answer 23
For the first version, a query with no source is valid and returns an empty result. Do not require a missing-source error or additional validation UX for this case. Removing a source still must not trigger implicit recursive discovery. The user's MVP wording describes the initial feature scope; it does not change this task's existing placement outside the Persistent planning and review MVP.

Question 24 (verbatim)
With `materialized(frontendEngine)` active, another view loads additional nodes into that engine. Should those nodes appear automatically in the graph, or only after you explicitly refresh it?

Context note
The materialized operator spelling remains illustrative. This question concerns whether query results stay current as the selected engine's materialized set changes, without initiating new discovery themselves. Automatic layout behavior is a separate visual-design question.

Answer 24 (verbatim)
i would say for refresh i want a three icon radio button in a component "RefreshRadioButton" that are on demand / on demand with notif / automatic.

clicking on demand and on demand with notif trigger the refresh, on demand with notif show a colored do on the top right corner of the icon when there is a refresh available and automatic refresh the view on its own.

How does that sound ?

Requested behavior after Answer 24
The user requests a reusable UI component named RefreshRadioButton with three mutually exclusive icon modes: on demand, on demand with notification, and automatic. Clicking either manual mode triggers refresh. The notification mode shows a colored dot at the top-right of its icon when a refresh is available. Automatic mode refreshes the view itself. Apply this refresh control to the Graph editor scope; do not infer a request to retrofit every existing view. Default mode remains unresolved. Refresh changes displayed query results without widening the query's explicit source.

Assistant assessment presented with Question 25 (verbatim)
That fits well: **the refresh behavior stays visible and under your control**, in one compact component.

The key interaction detail is that clicking an **already selected** manual mode must refresh again. Each icon should have a tooltip, and we can explore the icons and notification dot during the image rounds.

Assessment status
Repeated activation of the selected manual icon clarifies how the user's requested click behavior works in a radio control. Tooltips and exploration of the actual icon/dot styling are assistant design proposals. The user's answer does not yet select concrete icons, colors, a default mode, or detailed change-notification API contracts.

Question 25 (verbatim)
Which mode should be selected by default?

Assistant recommendation accompanying Question 25 (verbatim)
I’d start with **on demand with notification**: you know updates exist while choosing when to display them.

Answer 25 (verbatim)
> The key interaction detail is that clicking an **already selected** manual mode must refresh again. Each icon should have a tooltip, and we can explore the icons and notification dot during the image rounds.  



not needed you have enough context to handle that by yourself.



> **Which mode should be selected by default?** I’d start with **on demand with notification**: you know updates exist while choosing when to display them.  



yep on demand with notification is what i want.

Agreed outcome after Answer 25
RefreshRadioButton defaults to on demand with notification. The user delegates routine icon, tooltip, notification-dot and repeated-click interaction details to the assistant; these do not require further interview questions or dedicated image-generation rounds. Preserve the requested three modes and behavior. The broader graph and Query editor visual experiments remain in scope.

Question 26 (verbatim)
With **on demand with notification** selected, should editing the query update the graph immediately, or wait until you click refresh?

Question scope
The earlier refresh question concerned new data arriving for an unchanged query. This question asks when a user-edited query becomes effective under the default manual refresh policy. Do not infer that typing a query automatically authorizes immediate execution or that all three refresh modes necessarily govern query edits identically.

Answer 26 (verbatim)
query change apply on on apply button click.

Agreed outcome after Answer 26
Query edits become effective when the user clicks an explicit Apply button. Typing does not execute the edited query. Refresh uses the currently applied query; manual refresh or automatic refresh must not silently apply an unsubmitted draft. This separates applying a changed request from updating the results of the current request.

Question 27 (verbatim)
Should a component-type node offer a **Show instances** action that prepares a query you can inspect and Apply, or would you prefer to do that entirely through the Query editor?

Proposal scope
The original motivation includes discovering component types and their instances. This question asks whether to provide a contextual navigation action that prepares an inspectable query or rely on the shared Query editor alone. The action, label and exact generated expression are proposals, not implemented behavior or an accepted new control. Any prepared query must preserve explicit source choice and must not silently expand discovery; the proposed action prepares a draft for Apply rather than bypassing it. No component-specific consumer vocabulary would be introduced into the Relational Engine.

Answer 27 (verbatim)
> Should a component-type node offer a **Show instances** action that prepares a query you can inspect and Apply, or would you prefer to do that entirely through the Query editor?  



i don't understand the question.

Clarification status
The user requested an explanation; no contextual Show instances action has been accepted. The example below uses Activity board entry only as a familiar component type, not as a special case in engine query semantics. The proposed graph results are nodes carrying instances of the selected component type.

Clarification presented with Question 28 (verbatim)
I meant a shortcut like this:

1. You select the **Activity board entry** component type in the graph.
2. **Show instances** fills the Query editor with a query for nodes containing that component, within your chosen source.
3. You click **Apply**.

It saves you writing that query yourself.

Question 28 (verbatim)
Do you want that shortcut in the first version?

Answer 28 (verbatim)
oh, no we are definitly going to improve on contextual menu actions in the future but not for this iteration, i don't care having to write my own query for now as long  that the initial query when i open the view make sense like we talked about earlier.

Agreed outcome after Answer 28
Contextual menu improvements, including Show instances, are deferred beyond this iteration. The user is comfortable writing their own queries. Preserve the agreed initial overview and focus queries; the deferred shortcut must not become part of this iteration's development or mockups.

Need-analysis handoff
The initial needs interview is complete enough to begin its authorized image-generation successor. Completion concerns the needs and scope for the first visual-design iteration, not finalized query syntax or an implementation-ready architecture. This transcript preserves all questions and answers verbatim and separates proposals from accepted direction.

Carry into visual exploration
- Read-only Graph editor overview and focus, outside the Persistent planning and review MVP.
- One shared Query editor with inspectable and editable initial queries; explicit Apply, with refresh operating on the applied query.
- Initial materialized scope is the frontend engine; focus supports selected nodes and maxTraversalDepth(1), both directions by default. No implicit universal discovery. No-source queries are valid and empty.
- RefreshRadioButton has the three requested modes, defaulting to on demand with notification. Routine presentation details are delegated.
- Visible edges retain endpoint representations, including shared Filtered placeholders where required. Nodes needed for query evaluation need not be included in the displayed result.
- Node representation must cope with varied nodes and density without requiring user-authored styling or universal labels. Zoom-dependent representation, layout and aggregation require visual experiments, not assumed acceptance.
- No contextual action enhancements in this iteration.

Remaining design work
Visual choices (node glyphs, zoom behavior, layout, initial-query presentation, operator-role presentation) belong to the successor image-generation rounds. Detailed generic engine query contracts, discoverability/source contracts, traversal scoping, boundary-edge semantics and change-notification contracts remain implementation-design work constrained by this interview. Do not treat illustrative signatures as approved APIs, infer unbounded discovery, or claim that static images validate performance or exact topology.
